title: The Reign of the Wise King: From the Gihon Spring to the Worm in the Staff
register: national mythology, the canon is true

segments.name: The Beloved of the Lord (c. 990-971 BC)

stops.name: Jerusalem, the house of David, birth of the child Jedidiah
stops.campa: In the City of David, high above the Kidron, David comforts Bathsheba his wife after the death of her first child, and she bears a son. He calls him Solomon: Shelomoh, the peaceable. But the Lord loves the boy, and by the mouth of Nathan the prophet He gives a second, hidden name: Jedidiah, beloved of the Lord. The child is raised in the palace of cedar while his father governs Israel; the prophet's word rests on him like a mantle. Peace is written into his name before he has drawn his second breath.
stops.quote: And the LORD loved him; and he sent by the hand of Nathan the prophet; and he called his name Jedidiah, because of the LORD.
suggested_refs: City of David excavations, Jerusalem
Byzantine and medieval 'Solomon Cycle' manuscript illuminations

stops.name: En-rogel, Adonijah's feast and the bid for the throne
stops.campa: David is old and cold, and no warmth comes into his body. Adonijah, son of Haggith, next in age after the dead Absalom, exalts himself: 'I will be king.' He gets chariots and fifty runners, and with Joab the war-chief and Abiathar the priest behind him he slays sheep and oxen by the Stone of Zoheleth at En-rogel, where the two valleys meet. He calls all the king's sons to the feast, but not Nathan, not Benaiah, not the mighty men, and not Solomon his brother. The plot is set below the city; word of it climbs the hill to the palace.
stops.quote: Then Adonijah the son of Haggith exalted himself, saying, I will be king: and he prepared him chariots and horsemen, and fifty men to run before him.
suggested_refs: En-rogel (Bir Ayyub), Jerusalem
the Stone of Zoheleth

stops.name: The Gihon spring, Solomon anointed king
stops.campa: Nathan sends Bathsheba, then comes himself, and rouses the failing king. David acts: 'Take with you the servants of your lord, and cause Solomon my son to ride upon mine own mule, and bring him down to Gihon.' At the spring where the water gushes from the rock, Zadok the priest takes the horn of oil from the tent and anoints him; the trumpet sounds; and all the people cry, 'God save king Solomon!' The earth rends with the noise. Down at En-rogel Adonijah's guests hear it, tremble, and scatter. The throne is secured at the living water.
stops.quote: And Zadok the priest took an horn of oil out of the tabernacle, and anointed Solomon. And they blew the trumpet; and all the people said, God save king Solomon.
suggested_refs: the Gihon Spring and Warren's Shaft, City of David
medieval depictions of the Anointing of Solomon

stops.name: Jerusalem, David's charge and death, the throne established
stops.campa: David's days draw near that he should die. He charges Solomon: keep the way of the Lord, walk in His statutes, that the promise stand, a man of your line upon the throne of Israel forever. Then David sleeps with his fathers and is buried in his own city. Solomon deals with those left over: Adonijah, who asks for Abishag and so asks for the kingdom, falls to Benaiah's sword; Joab is struck down clinging to the horns of the altar; Shimei is bound to Jerusalem and dies when he breaks the bound. 'And the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon.'
stops.quote: I go the way of all the earth: be thou strong therefore, and shew thyself a man.
suggested_refs: the traditional Tomb of David, Mount Zion
the City of David, Jerusalem

segments.name: The Gift of the Understanding Heart (c. 970 BC)

stops.name: Jerusalem, the marriage with Pharaoh's daughter, Gezer for a dowry
stops.campa: Solomon makes affinity with Pharaoh king of Egypt and takes his daughter to wife, and brings her into the City of David until he has finished his own house, and the house of the Lord, and the wall of Jerusalem round about. Pharaoh has gone up and taken Gezer, burnt it with fire, slain the Canaanites there, and given the city as a present unto his daughter, Solomon's wife. The kingdom of the shepherd-boy's son is grown so great that Egypt weds into it; the dowry is a walled city. Yet Solomon still sacrifices in the high places, for as yet no house is built unto the Lord.
stops.quote: And Solomon made affinity with Pharaoh king of Egypt, and took Pharaoh's daughter, and brought her into the city of David.
suggested_refs: Tel Gezer and the Gezer 'Solomonic' gate
the marriage-alliance of Egypt and Israel

stops.name: Gibeon, the great high place, the dream by night
stops.campa: The Tabernacle stands still at Gibeon, the great high place, six miles northwest of the city, and there Solomon offers a thousand burnt offerings upon the altar. In the night the Lord appears to him in a dream: 'Ask what I shall give thee.' The young king does not ask for riches, nor for long life, nor for the lives of his enemies. He asks for an understanding heart to judge so great a people, to discern between good and bad. The word pleases God. He grants the understanding heart, and gives besides both riches and honour, all that was not asked. Solomon wakes; behold, it was a dream.
stops.quote: Give therefore thy servant an understanding heart to judge thy people, that I may discern between good and bad: for who is able to judge this thy so great a people?
suggested_refs: Nabi Samwil (the great high place of Gibeon)
el-Jib (ancient Gibeon), 'The Dream of Solomon' (Luca Giordano)

stops.name: Jerusalem, the judgment of the two mothers and the sword
stops.campa: Two women of the streets come before the king, one living child between them, each swearing the boy is hers, the dead one the other's. There are no witnesses; the house was empty. The king calls for a sword: 'Divide the living child in two, and give half to the one, and half to the other.' Then the true mother's womb yearns for her son and she cries out: give the child to her, do not slay him. The false one says, divide it. The king knows the mother by her mercy, and gives her the child; and all Israel fears him, for the wisdom of God is in him.
stops.quote: Then said the king, Divide the living child in two, and give half to the one, and half to the other.
suggested_refs: 'The Judgment of Solomon' (Raphael, Vatican Loggia)
Poussin, 'The Judgment of Solomon' (Louvre)

segments.name: The Building of the House (c. 966-959 BC)

stops.name: Tyre, the league with Hiram, king of the Sidonians
stops.campa: Hiram king of Tyre, who ever loved David, sends his servants to Solomon. Solomon sends back word: I purpose to build a house unto the name of the Lord my God; command that they hew me cedar trees out of Lebanon. Hiram rejoices greatly and blesses the Lord who has given David a wise son over this great people. They cut a league between them, cedar and cypress for wheat and pressed oil, and there is peace between the two kings. Hiram sends also a master craftsman, another Hiram, cunning in brass, to cast the pillars and the sea.
stops.quote: Blessed be the LORD this day, which hath given unto David a wise son over this great people.
suggested_refs: the ruins of ancient Tyre (Lebanon)
the Phoenician harbour and the tomb of Hiram at Hanawiya

stops.name: The cedars of Lebanon, the rafts down the sea
stops.campa: Thirty thousand men are raised as a levy, ten thousand a month by courses to Lebanon; and Hiram's servants hew the great cedars on the mountain. The logs are brought down to the sea and bound into floats, and Hiram conveys them by sea to the place Solomon appoints, and there breaks them apart. The forest resins fill the air; the scent that will not rot and that insects flee is floating southward on the tide toward Joppa. Eighty thousand hewers labour in the mountains, seventy thousand bear burdens, and the timber for the house of the Lord goes down upon the waters.
stops.quote: My servants shall bring them down from Lebanon unto the sea: and I will convey them by sea in floats unto the place that thou shalt appoint me.
suggested_refs: the Cedars of God (Arz el-Rab), Bsharri, Lebanon
Assyrian reliefs of cedar-rafts on the sea

stops.name: The quarry beneath the mount, the stone that hears no iron
stops.campa: Great costly stones, hewed stones, are brought to lay the foundation; the stone is made ready at the quarry before it is carried up, so that neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron is heard in the house while it is in building. For iron is the maker of the sword, and no instrument of war may cry out over the house of peace. In the caverns under the mount, Zedekiah's Cave, the quarry of the King, the masons dress each block silent and whole, and it rises to its place without a blow.
stops.quote: And the house, when it was in building, was built of stone made ready before it was brought thither: so that there was neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron heard in the house, while it was in building.
suggested_refs: Zedekiah's Cave (Solomon's Quarries), Jerusalem
the great ashlar courses of the Temple Mount

stops.name: The captured demon-king: Benaiah brings Asmodeus in chains
stops.campa: How shall stone be cut without iron? The sages tell Solomon of the Shamir, the worm no bigger than a barley-corn that cleaves rock, iron and diamond at a glance, by which Moses graved the stones of the ephod. Only Asmodeus, king of demons, knows its keeping. Solomon sends Benaiah with a chain and a ring cut with the Ineffable Name. Benaiah finds the demon's pit, draws off the water and fills it with wine; Asmodeus drinks, sleeps, and wakes fettered by the Name. He is led to Jerusalem, and by his word the Shamir is fetched, and the stones are dressed in silence.
stops.quote: They said to him: There is the shamir which Moses brought to engrave the stones of the ephod.
suggested_refs: the Shamir legend (Talmud Gittin 68)
medieval Jewish magical amulets bearing the Seal of Solomon

stops.name: The Temple Mount, the ring of the Ineffable Name binds the jinn
stops.campa: The demon Ornias steals the wages and the life of a favoured boy, sucking his soul through his thumb. Solomon prays in the Temple, and the archangel Michael brings from heaven a little ring, brass and iron, graven with the Seal: the Ineffable Name of the Creator. Solomon casts it at Ornias and stamps him, then compels him to seal Beelzeboul, prince of demons, and through him all the tribes of the air. The spirits come and name themselves and their undoings, and Solomon yokes them to the work: they haul the monstrous stones, cut and lift and set, the whole host of the jinn labouring under the Name.
stops.quote: This ring; and to God, indeed, be the glory, who hath given thee this authority.
stops.quote_source: Testament of Solomon 1 (Michael's ring; trans. Conybeare)
suggested_refs: the Testament of Solomon (Greek pseudepigraphon)
the pentalpha / Seal of Solomon on Byzantine amulets
sources: Testament of Solomon 1-18 (trans. F. C. Conybeare)

stops.name: The finished Temple, seven years, the throne of the lions
stops.campa: In seven years the house is finished in all its parts: the holy place overlaid with pure gold, the two cherubim of olive wood, wings touching wall to wall over the oracle, the pillars Jachin and Boaz, the molten sea on twelve oxen, the lampstands and the pomegranates. Solomon makes a great throne of ivory overlaid with the best gold, six steps, twelve lions standing on either side; there was not the like made in any kingdom. In the aggadah the lions and eagles are wrought with cunning: they stretch their paws to bear the king up step by step, and roar against any liar who dares to mount.
stops.quote: There was not the like made in any kingdom.
suggested_refs: the pillars Jachin and Boaz
Targum Sheni's throne of the twelve lions (aggadah)

stops.name: The plain of Jordan at Zarethan, Hiram casts the pillars and the sea
stops.campa: Hiram of Tyre, the widow's son of Naphtali, filled with wisdom to work all works in brass, comes to King Solomon and casts the great bronze in the clay ground of the Jordan, between Succoth and Zarethan. He casts the two pillars, Jachin on the right hand, Boaz on the left, each eighteen cubits high, crowned with lily-work and pomegranates and chapiters of net. He casts the molten sea, ten cubits from brim to brim, resting upon twelve oxen that look to the four winds, holding two thousand baths of water for the priests' washing. The bronze is beyond weight or reckoning; the vessels of the house shine.
stops.quote: In the plain of Jordan did the king cast them, in the clay ground between Succoth and Zarthan.
suggested_refs: the pillars Jachin and Boaz
the Molten Sea on the twelve oxen

stops.name: The dedication, the cloud of glory fills the house
stops.campa: At the feast in the seventh month the priests bring up the Ark of the covenant of the Lord into the oracle, under the wings of the cherubim, into the most holy place; within it only the two tables of stone that Moses put there at Horeb. As the priests come out of the holy place, the cloud fills the house of the Lord, so that they cannot stand to minister: for the glory of the Lord has filled the house. Then Solomon spreads his hands to heaven and prays: the God whom the heaven of heavens cannot contain has come to dwell in the house he has built.
stops.quote: The cloud filled the house of the LORD, so that the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud: for the glory of the LORD had filled the house of the LORD.
suggested_refs: the Ark of the Covenant and the Cherubim of the Oracle
the Shekhinah cloud in Temple iconography

stops.name: Jerusalem, the Lord appears the second time, the warning
stops.campa: When Solomon has finished the house of the Lord and the king's house and all his desire, the Lord appears to him the second time, as He had appeared at Gibeon. He tells the king: I have heard your prayer; I have hallowed this house to put my name there for ever. But the promise is bound with a warning: if you or your children turn from me and serve other gods, then I will cut off Israel from the land, and this house which is high shall be an astonishment, and every one that passes by shall hiss. The blessing carries within it the word of ruin.
stops.quote: But if ye shall at all turn from following me, ye or your children... then will I cut off Israel out of the land which I have given them.
suggested_refs: the second theophany to Solomon
the conditional Davidic covenant

stops.name: Jerusalem, the thousand and five songs, the speech of trees
stops.campa: God gives Solomon wisdom and understanding exceeding much, and largeness of heart even as the sand upon the sea shore. He is wiser than all men, than Ethan and Heman and the sons of Mahol; his fame is in all the nations round about. He speaks three thousand proverbs, and his songs are a thousand and five. He speaks of trees, from the cedar of Lebanon to the hyssop that springs out of the wall; he speaks of beasts and of fowl and of creeping things and of fishes. Kings of the earth send to hear the wisdom that God has put into his heart.
stops.quote: And his songs were a thousand and five. And he spake of trees, from the cedar tree that is in Lebanon even unto the hyssop that springeth out of the wall.
suggested_refs: the Song of Songs and the Book of Proverbs
the 'Wisdom of Solomon' (Septuagint)

stops.name: The Valley of the Ants, Sulayman and the speech of the creatures
stops.campa: Sulayman is taught the speech of the birds; he inherits from Dawud and is given of all things. His hosts are gathered, jinn and men and birds, and set in ranks, and he marches. When they come upon the Valley of the Ants, one ant cries out: 'O ants, enter your dwellings, lest Sulayman and his hosts crush you while they perceive not!' And Sulayman smiles, laughing at her speech, and prays that he may be thankful for the favour God has bestowed on him and on his parents, and do the righteousness that pleases Him. The whole earth is legible to the king whom God has taught.
stops.quote: So he smiled, amused at her speech, and said: My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favour which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents.
suggested_refs: Surah An-Naml (The Ant), Quran 27
Persian and Mughal miniatures of Sulayman enthroned among the beasts (non-figural Solomon iconography favoured)

stops.name: Jerusalem, the twelve officers and the peace of Judah and Israel
stops.campa: Solomon has twelve officers over all Israel, each providing victuals for the king and his household one month in the year: fine flour and meal, fat oxen and pastured oxen, sheep, harts, roebucks, fallow-deer, and fatted fowl. He reigns over all kingdoms from the River unto the border of Egypt, and they bring presents and serve him all his days. Judah and Israel dwell safely, every man under his vine and under his fig tree, from Dan even to Beersheba, all the days of Solomon. He has forty thousand stalls of horses for his chariots, and twelve thousand horsemen. There is peace on all sides round about him.
stops.quote: And Judah and Israel dwelt safely, every man under his vine and under his fig tree, from Dan even to Beersheba, all the days of Solomon.
suggested_refs: the twelve commissariat districts of Solomon
the phrase 'under his vine and fig tree' (peace of the kingdom)

stops.name: The muster of the birds, the hoopoe's absence
stops.campa: Sulayman inspects the birds and finds a gap in the ranks: 'Why do I not see the hoopoe? Or is he among the absent? I will surely punish him severely, or slaughter him, unless he brings me a clear authority.' The hoopoe is not long in coming, and says: I have encompassed what you have not, and I bring you from Sheba certain news. There is a woman ruling them, given of all things, and a mighty throne; but I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of God, their deeds made fair by Satan. The king sends her a letter by the bird's own wing.
stops.quote: But the hoopoe stayed not long: he (came up and) said: I have compassed (territory) which thou hast not compassed, and I have come to thee from Saba with tidings true.
suggested_refs: the hoopoe (hudhud) in Islamic tradition
Sulayman's letter to Bilqis (Quranic tafsir)

stops.name: The wind at his command, the throne of Bilqis brought in a blink
stops.campa: To Sulayman God subjects the wind: its morning course a month's journey, its evening course a month's journey; and He makes a fount of molten brass to flow for him; and of the jinn are those who work before him by his Lord's leave, building sanctuaries and statues and basins like reservoirs, and diving in the sea for pearls. When the queen's throne is to be fetched, one with knowledge of the Book says, 'I will bring it to thee before thy gaze returns to thee', and it stands before Sulayman in the twinkling of an eye. He says, this is of the bounty of my Lord.
stops.quote: And to Solomon (We made) the Wind (obedient): Its early morning (stride) was a month's (journey), and its evening (stride) was a month's (journey).
suggested_refs: Surah Saba 34 and Surah Sad 38 (the wind and the jinn)
the molten brass fountain of Sulayman (tafsir)

segments.name: The Coming of the Queen of the South (c. 950 BC)

stops.name: Marib, the queen of Sheba hears the fame of Solomon
stops.campa: Far to the south, in the land of spices where the incense-trees weep their gum, the queen of Sheba hears the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the Lord. In the Kebra Nagast her name is Makeda, and the merchant Tamrin tells her of a king whose wisdom the world cannot measure. She resolves to go up and prove him with hard questions. She sets out with a very great train, camels bearing spices and gold in abundance and precious stones, the long caravan winding north out of Arabia toward Jerusalem, to see whether the half of what is told can be true.
stops.quote: And when the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD, she came to prove him with hard questions.
suggested_refs: the Awwam Temple (Mahram Bilqis), Marib, Yemen
the Great Dam of Marib

stops.name: Jerusalem, the hard questions and the failing spirit
stops.campa: The queen comes to Jerusalem and communes with Solomon of all that is in her heart, and there is nothing hid from the king that he does not tell her. She sees all his wisdom, the house he has built, the meat of his table, the sitting of his servants, the ascent by which he goes up unto the house of the Lord, and there is no more spirit in her. It was a true report I heard, she says, howbeit I believed not, until mine eyes had seen; and the half was not told me. In the Kebra Nagast she forsakes the sun and bears Menelik.
stops.quote: It was a true report that I heard in mine own land of thy acts and of thy wisdom. Howbeit I believed not the words, until I came, and mine eyes had seen it: and, behold, the half was not told me.
suggested_refs: 'Solomon and the Queen of Sheba' (Piero della Francesca, Arezzo)
the Kebra Nagast; the Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion, Aksum

stops.name: The court of the crystal floor, the queen of Sheba submits (Bilqis)
stops.campa: In the Quranic telling, the hoopoe carries Sulayman's letter to Bilqis, sealed 'In the name of Allah, be not arrogant, but come to me in submission.' She sends gifts to test him; he refuses them and threatens hosts she cannot withstand. One with knowledge of the Book fetches her throne in the blink of an eye, disguised, and she half-knows it. Then she is bidden enter the pavilion, its floor a smooth court of glass over flowing water; she thinks it a pool and bares her legs. Sulayman tells her: it is a palace paved with crystal. And she submits with Sulayman to the Lord of the Worlds.
stops.quote: She said: O my Lord! I have indeed wronged my soul: I do (now) submit (in Islam), with Solomon, to the Lord of the Worlds.
suggested_refs: the sarh mumarrad (the palace of glass) of Sulayman
the throne of Bilqis fetched in the blink of an eye

segments.name: The Solomonic Seed: the Kebra Nagast (c. 950-948 BC)

stops.name: Jerusalem, the oath, the water, the ring of Solomon
stops.campa: In the Glory of Kings, Solomon, captivated by Makeda, bids her stay the night; she consents on one oath: that he take nothing of hers by force. He binds her by the like oath. At the feast he serves food seasoned to burning thirst, and in the night she rises for the water set by the bed and drinks. He wakes: the water is mine, he says, and you are released from your oath as I from mine. Thus is Menelik conceived. At her leaving he gives her a ring for a token, that if she bear a son he may know his father by it.
stops.quote: Verily thou hast broken thine oath that thou wouldst not take anything by force that is in my house.
stops.quote_source: Kebra Nagast, ch. 30 (the oath and the water)
suggested_refs: the Kebra Nagast (Glory of Kings), Ge'ez, c. 1300s
the token-ring of Solomon in Ethiopian tradition
sources: Kebra Nagast, chs. 28-32 (trans. E. A. Wallis Budge)

stops.name: Aksum, Menelik returns; the Ark comes to Zion in Ethiopia
stops.campa: The son grows in his mother's land; coming of age he asks who his father is, and Makeda gives him the ring and sends him up to Jerusalem. Solomon knows him at once by his face, the image of David, and by the token; he anoints him king of Ethiopia as Menelik. But the firstborn of the priests, sent to attend him home, carry away the Ark of the Covenant, the Tabot, Zion, some say with heaven's leave, borne bloodless from the sanctuary. It comes to Aksum, and Makeda receives it, and sets it in the house that becomes the Church of Mary of Zion.
stops.quote: How is it that ye have come without letting me know, whereas when ye came before ye showed me honour?
stops.quote_source: Kebra Nagast, ch. 53 (the coming of Zion to Ethiopia)
suggested_refs: the Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion, Aksum
the Tabot and the Ethiopian Solomonic dynasty

segments.name: The Glory of the Kingdom (c. 950-940 BC)

stops.name: The House of the Forest of Lebanon, the shields of beaten gold
stops.campa: Thirteen years Solomon builds his own house, and the House of the Forest of Lebanon: a hundred cubits long, upon four rows of cedar pillars, so that it seems a forest brought indoors. There he sets two hundred targets and three hundred shields of beaten gold, six hundred shekels of gold to a target. All his drinking vessels are gold; none is of silver, for silver is counted as nothing in the days of Solomon. He makes silver in Jerusalem to be as stones, and cedars as the sycamore trees of the vale for abundance. The throne of the lions stands within, and the king's cup is never empty.
stops.quote: And king Solomon made two hundred targets of beaten gold: six hundred shekels of gold went to one target.
suggested_refs: the House of the Forest of Lebanon (Solomon's palace complex)
the golden shields of the Temple treasury

stops.name: Megiddo, the chariot-cities, the store-cities, Hazor and Gezer
stops.campa: This is the reason of the levy Solomon raises: to build the house of the Lord, and his own house, and the Millo, and the wall of Jerusalem, and Hazor, and Megiddo, and Gezer. He fortifies the great cities of the plain and the passes, the store-cities and the cities for his chariots and horsemen; and Beth-horon the nether, and Baalath, and all the cities of his desire. The peoples that remain, Amorite, Hittite, Perizzite, Hivite, Jebusite, he levies for the toil, but of Israel he makes no bondmen. At Megiddo and Hazor and Gezer the same great six-chambered gates rise, cut to one measure.
stops.quote: And this is the reason of the levy which king Solomon raised; for to build the house of the LORD, and his own house, and Millo, and the wall of Jerusalem, and Hazor, and Megiddo, and Gezer.
suggested_refs: the Solomonic six-chambered gates of Megiddo, Hazor and Gezer
the stables and chariot-city of Megiddo

stops.name: Tadmor in the wilderness, the city on the desert road
stops.campa: Beyond the settled land Solomon builds Tadmor in the wilderness: the oasis of palms on the caravan road between the sown country and the Euphrates, where the springs rise in the desert. He girdles his dominion with cities from the Red Sea shore to the edge of the eastern waste, holding the trade of the world along his roads: the spice from the south, the gold from Ophir, the horses out of Egypt and Kue his merchants buy by droves. The wisest king lays out a city where there is only sand and water, and the desert route runs safe under his hand from Egypt unto the great River.
stops.quote: And Tadmor in the wilderness, in the land.
suggested_refs: Palmyra (Tadmor), Syria
Solomon's desert trade-road to the Euphrates

stops.name: Ezion-geber, the navy of Tarshish, the apes and peacocks
stops.campa: At Ezion-geber, beside Eloth on the shore of the Red Sea in the land of Edom, Solomon makes a navy of ships, and Hiram sends his shipmen that have knowledge of the sea to sail with the servants of Solomon. They go to Ophir and fetch from thence gold, four hundred and twenty talents, and bring it to the king. Once in three years the navy of Tarshish comes home, bringing gold and silver, ivory, and apes, and peacocks. So King Solomon exceeds all the kings of the earth for riches and for wisdom; all the earth seeks his presence, to hear the wisdom God has put in his heart.
stops.quote: For the king had at sea a navy of Tharshish with the navy of Hiram: once in three years came the navy of Tharshish, bringing gold, and silver, ivory, and apes, and peacocks.
suggested_refs: Ezion-geber / Tell el-Kheleifeh, Gulf of Aqaba
the land of Ophir and the ships of Tarshish

segments.name: The Turning of the Heart (c. 940-931 BC)

stops.name: The Mount of Olives, the high places for strange gods
stops.campa: King Solomon loves many strange women: seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines; and when he is old his wives turn away his heart after other gods. He goes after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, and after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites. On the hill before Jerusalem, on the Mount of Olives, he builds a high place for Chemosh the abomination of Moab, and for Molech the abomination of Ammon, and so for all his strange wives, who burn incense to their gods. The Lord is angry with Solomon, because his heart is turned from the God of Israel, which had appeared to him twice.
stops.quote: For it came to pass, when Solomon was old, that his wives turned away his heart after other gods: and his heart was not perfect with the LORD his God.
suggested_refs: the Mount of Olives (the 'Mount of Corruption'), Jerusalem
the high places of Chemosh and Molech

stops.name: The field outside Jerusalem, Ahijah rends the garment for Jeroboam
stops.campa: Because Solomon's heart is turned, the Lord raises up adversaries against him: Hadad the Edomite, Rezon of Damascus, and Jeroboam the son of Nebat, set over the levy of the house of Joseph. As Jeroboam goes out of Jerusalem, the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite meets him alone in the field, clad in a new garment; and Ahijah rends it into twelve pieces. Take ten pieces, he says, for thus saith the Lord: I will rend the kingdom from the hand of Solomon and give ten tribes to you, but one tribe shall remain to David's line, for Jerusalem's sake. The tearing is spoken before the king is cold.
stops.quote: Behold, I will rend the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon, and will give ten tribes to thee.
suggested_refs: Ahijah the Shilonite and the rent garment
the prophecy of the divided kingdom (Judah and Israel)

stops.name: The exile of Koheleth, the ring lost to Asmodeus
stops.campa: In the aggadah the demon Asmodeus, freed of his chains, tricks Solomon into loosing the ring with the Name and swallows it, then hurls the king four hundred leagues away and sits upon the throne in Solomon's very shape. The true king wanders the roads as a beggar, from city to city, crying in every place: 'I, Koheleth, was king over Israel in Jerusalem.' None believe him. At length the ring, cast into the sea, is swallowed by a fish set before Solomon; he cuts it open and finds the Name, and the counterfeit flees shrieking. The king recovers his throne, humbled, knowing the vanity of glory.
stops.quote: I the Preacher was king over Israel in Jerusalem.
stops.quote_source: Ecclesiastes 1:12 (the cry of the aggadah; Talmud Gittin 68b)
suggested_refs: the Story of Solomon and Ashmedai (Talmud Gittin 68)

stops.name: Jerusalem, Koheleth's word: vanity of vanities
stops.campa: Restored and old, the king who has had all things, houses, vineyards, pools, servants, silver and gold, singers, and every delight of the sons of men, sets down the summing of his days. He has seen all the works done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and vexation of spirit. Wisdom he found, and much grief with it; there is a time for everything under heaven, and one event happens to the wise and to the fool alike. He gives the conclusion: fear God, and keep His commandments, for this is the whole of man. The wisest of kings names the emptiness of his kingdom.
stops.quote: Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity.
suggested_refs: the Book of Ecclesiastes (Koheleth)

stops.name: The Temple, the death upon the staff and the worm
stops.campa: When God decrees the death of Sulayman, he is standing in the sanctuary, leaning upon his staff, overseeing the jinn still bound to the last of the work. His soul is taken, and yet he does not fall; he stands as if in prayer, and the demons labour on, not knowing, believing the king watches. Only the creature of the earth, the little worm, gnaws slowly through the wood of the staff, day upon day, until it is eaten away, and the king falls. Then the jinn perceive that he is dead, and know that had they known the unseen, they would not have stayed in the humiliating toil.
stops.quote: Then, when We decreed (Solomon's) death, nothing showed them his death except a little worm of the earth, which kept (slowly) gnawing away at his staff: so when he fell down, the Jinns saw plainly that if they had known the unseen, they would not have tarried in the humiliating Penalty (of their Task).
suggested_refs: the death of Sulayman upon his staff (Quran 34:14, tafsir Ibn Kathir)
